answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The idea is authentically Kierkegaard’s — it appears in his 1843 journal (entry JJ:167, older cataloguing IV A 164), preserved in Søren Kierkegaards Skrifter. But this crisp one-liner is a later condensed paraphrase. The standard translation by Alexander Dru reads “life must be understood backwards … it must be lived forwards,” folded into a longer sentence — not the tidy aphorism usually quoted. So: right author, real source, smoothed wording.

source.excerpt: It is perfectly true, as the philosophers say, that life must be understood backwards. But they forget the other proposition, that it must be lived forwards.
trail: The exact source is a journal entry from 1843, catalogued JJ:167 (older numbering IV A 164) in Søren Kierkegaards Skrifter, vol. 18 ↗.

The Danish original reads “…Livet maa forstaaes baglænds … det maa leves forlænds,” standardly translated by Alexander Dru as “life must be understood backwards … it must be lived forwards” (WIST Quotations ↗).
Wikiquote ↗ lists the crisp popular wording among ‘variants’ and WIST labels it “commonly paraphrased” — confirming the aphorism is a later condensation, not Kierkegaard’s literal line.
source.excerptNote: Alexander Dru’s 1938 translation of the 1843 journal entry. The popular one-line form — “Life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards” — is a condensation of this, not a literal rendering.
source.rightsNote: Kierkegaard’s Danish journal entry dates to 1843 and its original text is long in the public domain. But the English wording shown is a translation matter: the standard translation by Alexander Dru was first published in 1938 and is in copyright, while the specific crisp popular phrasing is an anonymous condensation of uncertain origin. Because no single public-domain edition carries this exact wording, we do not assert public-domain status.

author.name: Søren Kierkegaard
author.heading: About Søren Kierkegaard
author.metaLine: 1813–1855 · Danish philosopher, theologian & father of existentialism
author.bio: Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855) was a Danish philosopher and theologian, widely regarded as the first existentialist thinker. Alongside published works such as Either/Or and Fear and Trembling, he kept voluminous private journals; this reflection comes from a journal entry of 1843, the year of his most intense output. Many of his best-known ‘quotes’ circulate today in paraphrased forms drawn from those journals rather than as his exact words.

misattribution.heading: Right author, smoothed words
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of a stolen quote — the thought really is Kierkegaard’s. What has drifted is the wording: the internet’s tidy aphorism is a paraphrase of a longer, more tentative journal sentence.

items.why: Kierkegaard’s actual sentence, in Alexander Dru’s 1938 translation, is “It is perfectly true, as the philosophers say, that life must be understood backwards. But they forget the other proposition, that it must be lived forwards.” The crisp “Life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards” is a smoothed later condensation, flagged as a paraphrase by both WIST ↗ and Wikiquote ↗.

The popular line drops Kierkegaard’s follow-on point — that life can never fully be understood in time because “at no particular moment can I find the necessary resting-place from which to understand it.” The aphorism keeps the neat symmetry and loses the doubt (quote-source page ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution to Kierkegaard is correct and the source is documented (journal entry JJ:167, 1843); the popular exact wording is a later condensed paraphrase rather than his literal words — see WIST’s note ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Kierkegaard jotted this in a private journal in 1843, not for publication. It captures a genuine asymmetry of human experience: meaning tends to arrive in hindsight, yet we are forced to act while the future is still dark. That tension — understanding runs backward, living runs forward — is why the line reads as existentialist decades before the label existed.

In his fuller entry, Kierkegaard pushes further than the aphorism admits: because there is never a still ‘resting-place’ in time, life can never be completely understood even in retrospect. The popular one-liner keeps the elegant symmetry and quietly discards that unease.
context.pull: Understood backwards, lived forwards — but, Kierkegaard adds, never fully understood at all.
